prompt: An EMR on EC2 cluster is up for an hour. What is billed for each of its machines?
hint: Whose machine is it, and whose software?

choices.text: The EMR fee alone, because the fee includes the machine
choices.why: The fee is what EMR adds on top; the price sheet says so beside its line, and the machine is priced by EC2.

choices.text: The EC2 hour and the EMR fee
choices.why: Right: 0.32130 for an on-demand m7i.xlarge plus 0.05040 of fee, 0.37170 an hour.

choices.text: A DPU-hour, as Glue bills it
choices.why: DPUs are Glue's unit; EMR on EC2 bills machines.

choices.text: Only the EC2 hour: the software on it is open source, so EMR adds nothing
choices.why: Spark is open source, and EMR still charges for installing, configuring and running it on your machines.

prompt: Halfway through a job, AWS takes back one of the cluster's Spot task nodes. What happens to the job?
hint: What does a task node store?

choices.text: It fails, because the blocks of HDFS on that node are gone
choices.why: A task node runs no DataNode and holds no blocks; that loss belongs to a core node.

choices.text: The cluster terminates with it
choices.why: That is what losing the primary node does.

choices.text: Its tasks run again on another machine; slower, nothing lost
choices.why: Right. That is why task nodes are the ones put on Spot.

choices.text: EMR pauses the job until Spot capacity of the same type returns
choices.why: YARN does not pause; it gives the lost tasks to the machines it still has.

prompt: To save money, a team runs a six-hour nightly cluster with the primary, core and task nodes all on Spot. Which risk did they take that a Spot task group alone would not carry?
hint: Order the roles by what losing one costs.

choices.text: Spot prices rising past the on-demand price for the night
choices.why: With the maximum at the on-demand price, a group never pays more than on demand; when the market passes it, the machine is reclaimed instead.

choices.text: One reclaimed machine ending the whole night's run
choices.why: Right. A reclaimed primary ends the cluster, and a reclaimed core node can fail the job with its blocks.

choices.text: HDFS refusing to start on Spot machines
choices.why: HDFS runs on any machine; the problem is what happens when one goes.

choices.text: EMR charging a higher fee per hour on Spot machines
choices.why: The fee is the same however the machine is bought.

prompt: Why does a cluster that is created each night keep its data in S3 rather than in HDFS?
hint: Where does HDFS live?

choices.text: EMR cannot write Parquet into HDFS
choices.why: Spark writes Parquet to HDFS perfectly well; the problem is how long it stays.

choices.text: Reading S3 from EMR is free and reading HDFS is not
choices.why: Neither is the reason; HDFS is the cluster's own disks.

choices.text: Ending the cluster deletes its HDFS
choices.why: Right. HDFS lives on the core nodes' disks, and they go when the cluster goes.

choices.text: HDFS is slower than S3 for every kind of read
choices.why: Local disks are often faster; speed is not why a transient cluster avoids them.

prompt: Match each node to what it runs.
hint: Only one of them stores blocks of HDFS.

prompt: Quitanda's nightly cluster asks for Spot task nodes, and some nights it waits because m7i.xlarge Spot is short in the zone. What change addresses that?
hint: Spot is a set of pools, one per type and zone.

choices.text: Instance fleets offering three machine types for the task capacity
choices.why: Right. A fleet that can take any of several types draws from several pools, and rarely waits. It means rebuilding the cluster, since groups and fleets do not mix.

choices.text: A second instance group of m7i.xlarge Spot
choices.why: Same type, same zone, same pool: the shortage is the same.

choices.text: Moving the task nodes into the core group
choices.why: That puts HDFS on the machines that may vanish and does nothing about the shortage.

choices.text: A higher `BidPrice` on the same group
choices.why: A pool with no spare machines has none at any price; Spot is reclaimed by capacity, not auctioned.

prompt: In the lab, the cluster with fleets was created, and listing its fleets answered `500`. What is the right conclusion?
hint: What does a success from moto mean?

choices.text: Fleets are not offered in sa-east-1
choices.why: The region is not the issue; moto put the cluster in us-east-1 anyway.

choices.text: The request was well formed, and moto does not model fleets
choices.why: Right. `InstanceCollectionType` came back `null` too. How EMR fills a fleet was not run.

choices.text: The flags were wrong, and the cluster has no task nodes
choices.why: A malformed request is refused by the command line before it is sent; this one was accepted.

choices.text: A cluster's fleets take some minutes to appear
choices.why: moto waits for nothing; a 500 is an error inside moto, not a delay.

prompt: For a nightly batch job whose failure is merely annoying, which groups are sound candidates for Spot? Choose all that apply.
hint: Order the roles by what their loss costs.

choices.text: The task nodes
choices.why: Yes: losing one costs time.

choices.text: The core nodes, accepting that a reclaimed one can fail the run
choices.why: Yes, for a job allowed to fail; the section says core nodes should not be Spot unless the job can survive failing.

choices.text: The primary node, since it does none of the work
choices.why: It does none of the work and coordinates all of it; losing it ends the cluster.

choices.text: None of them: Spot is for stateless web servers
choices.why: Batch work that can be retried is the textbook use of Spot.

prompt: In moto, a Spark step pointing at a program in a bucket that does not exist is still `RUNNING` minutes later. What would the same step do on AWS?
hint: Who checks that the file exists?

choices.text: Stay `RUNNING` until the file is uploaded
choices.why: Nothing waits for the file; `spark-submit` looks for it once.

choices.text: Fail, with the reason in the logs under `--log-uri`
choices.why: Right. moto runs nothing, so it never reaches the moment the step would fail.

choices.text: Be refused by `add-steps` before it is queued
choices.why: A step's arguments are not checked when it is added; they are passed to the command.

choices.text: Report `COMPLETED`, because `spark-submit` itself started
choices.why: A step completes when its command succeeds, and this one cannot.

prompt: A cluster created with `--no-auto-terminate` that has finished its steps sits in the state ___, billed by the second.
hint: The describe-cluster output showed it.

prompt: Analysts query the curated data through Trino on weekdays from 9 to 18, and one nightly job runs at 3. Which arrangement fits both?
hint: One of the two has something to schedule around; the other does not.

choices.text: A long-running cluster with an idle timeout for the analysts, and a transient one per night for the job
choices.why: Right. Interactive work needs something running when people arrive; the job needs a cluster for an hour.

choices.text: A transient cluster for every analyst query
choices.why: Each query would wait for machines to boot and install; interactive work cannot be scheduled.

choices.text: One cluster left on all week for both
choices.why: It works, and it pays every night and weekend hour that nobody uses.

choices.text: Glue for the queries and EMR for the job
choices.why: Glue runs ETL jobs; it is not where analysts run interactive SQL.

prompt: An EMR Serverless application with no pre-initialised capacity has had no job for three days. What has it cost in compute?
hint: Look at `autoStopConfiguration`.

choices.text: Its minimum of workers for 72 hours
choices.why: With no pre-initialised capacity there is no minimum held.

choices.text: The EMR fee for every hour it existed
choices.why: Serverless has no per-hour fee for existing; it bills what jobs used.

choices.text: One DPU-hour a day to stay registered
choices.why: DPUs are Glue's unit, and nothing is billed for staying registered.

choices.text: Nothing: it stopped after 15 idle minutes
choices.why: Right. Serverless bills vCPU-hours and GB-hours that jobs used, and there were none.

prompt: When is EMR on EKS the right one of the three?
hint: It does not create machines.

choices.text: When the team has no Kubernetes and wants the simplest start
choices.why: Then it adds a Kubernetes cluster to operate just to run Spark.

choices.text: When Kubernetes already runs everything else
choices.why: Right. Spark then shares the nodes, the monitoring and the people the organisation already has.

choices.text: When the job keeps its data in HDFS between runs
choices.why: A virtual cluster has no HDFS of its own; that is EMR on EC2 with core nodes.

choices.text: When the goal is to pay for nothing between jobs, with no nodes of your own kept anywhere
choices.why: That is EMR Serverless; on EKS the nodes you keep cost what they cost.

prompt: Which of these did moto really do in this lesson's lab? Choose all that apply.
hint: Recording a request is not running it.

choices.text: Keep a step with its arguments, as `spark-submit` would receive them
choices.why: Yes; `list-steps` showed them.

choices.text: Keep the instance groups and the market each one pays in
choices.why: Yes; the table showed `SPOT` for the task group.

choices.text: Terminate the transient cluster after its step
choices.why: It stayed `WAITING` with the step `RUNNING`.

choices.text: Check that the EKS cluster behind the virtual cluster exists
choices.why: `aws eks list-clusters` was empty and the registration succeeded.

choices.text: Bill the Serverless job run for its vCPU-hours
choices.why: It reported 0.0 of everything.

prompt: An m7i.xlarge on demand is 0.32130 USD an hour and the EMR fee is 0.05040. What do one primary and four core nodes cost for 3 hours, in USD, to two decimals?
hint: Five machines, each the machine plus the fee, for three hours.

prompt: EMR on EC2 costs 0.37170 a unit-hour against Glue's 0.69000, and yet "EMR left on" is the most expensive line of the program. Why?
hint: Count the hours each line pays for.

choices.text: It pays all 730 hours of the month for 60 hours of work
choices.why: Right: eleven machines × 730 hours, worked or not.

choices.text: The EMR fee doubles on a cluster that runs longer than a day
choices.why: The fee per hour is the same on the first hour and the seven hundredth.

choices.text: It runs eleven machines where Glue runs ten
choices.why: One extra machine is 10%; the line is more than seven times Glue's.

choices.text: Spot machines are priced higher at night
choices.why: The program prices on-demand machines only, and the night is not the problem.

prompt: The cluster left on costs 2984.75 USD a month. Glue with ten DPUs costs 207.00 a month for each hour of nightly work. How many hours a night make the two equal? One decimal.
hint: Divide the flat line by the slope.

prompt: Order these by the price of one unit of 4 vCPU and 16 GB for an hour, cheapest first.
hint: Machine plus fee, reserved and on demand, then the per-job products.

prompt: Thirty more jobs would keep the same ten units busy sixteen hours a night. Which costs less a month: Glue with ten DPUs, or the cluster of eleven machines left on?
hint: Where do the two lines in the chart cross?

choices.text: Glue, at 207.00 for each nightly hour
choices.why: At sixteen hours that is 207.00 × 16 = 3312.00, above the flat line.

choices.text: The cluster left on, at 2984.75
choices.why: Right. Past 14.4 hours a night the flat line is below Glue's.

choices.text: Neither: at sixteen hours they cost the same
choices.why: They cost the same at 14.4 hours; at sixteen they have parted again.

choices.text: Glue, because a cluster also pays the minutes its machines take to boot
choices.why: A cluster left on boots once a month; those minutes are lost in 730 hours.

prompt: A Spark job runs once a month for forty minutes: ordinary ETL from catalogued tables, no special library. Which is the sensible home?
hint: Count the hours a cluster would wait.

choices.text: A long-running EMR cluster on reserved machines
choices.why: Reserved machines are paid all year for forty minutes a month of work.

choices.text: Glue
choices.why: Right: short, rare, ordinary and catalogued is the case Glue was built for.

choices.text: EMR on EKS
choices.why: Worth it where Kubernetes already exists, and nothing says it does here.

choices.text: A transient EMR cluster with Spot core nodes
choices.why: It works, and it costs a cluster definition and its upkeep to save cents on forty minutes.
